```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
    collapse = TRUE,
    comment = "#>",
    screenshot.force = FALSE,
    fig.align = "center",
    out.lines = 20
)

# the default output hook
hook_output <- knitr::knit_hooks$get("output")
knitr::knit_hooks$set(output = function(x, options) {
    if (!is.null(n <- options$out.lines)) {
        x <- unlist(strsplit(x, "\n", fixed = TRUE))
        if (length(x) > n) {
            # truncate the output
            x <- c(head(x, n), "....", "")
        } else {
            x <- c(x, "")
        }
        x <- paste(x, collapse = "\n") # paste first n lines together
    }
    hook_output(x, options)
})

options(crayon.enabled = FALSE)
options(data.table.print.class = TRUE)

library(eplusr)
```

This vignette introduces the `IdfGeometry` and `IdfViewer` classes.
`IdfGeometry` is designed to extract data for all geometry objects and perform
geometric operations on them, while `IdfViewer` displays IDF geometry in an
interactive Three.js/WebGL widget inspired by OpenStudio's geometry workflow.

---

# Extract all geometry data

All geometry data in an `Idf` object can be extracted using the
`Idf$geometry()`. What it returns is an `IdfGeometry` which parses all geometry
related objects, including:

* `GlobalGeometryRules`
* `Building`
* `Zone`
* All geometry related classes in the `Thermal Zones and Surfaces` group and
  `Daylighting` group

```{r}
eplus_ver <- max(avail_eplus())
eplus_ver

path_idf <- file.path(eplus_config(eplus_ver)$dir, "ExampleFiles/HospitalLowEnergy.idf")
idf <- read_idf(path_idf)
geom <- idf$geometry()
geom
```

# Get geometry data

## Get geometry rules

```{r}
geom$rules()
```

## Get surface area

```{r}
geom$area()
```

By default, `$area()` returns areas of all surfaces in current `Idf`. You can
specify `class` and `object` to only calculate objects of interest. This is
also true for the `$azimuth()` and `$tilt()` methods.

```{r}
geom$area(class = "Shading:Zone:Detailed")
```

With `net` being `TRUE`, the window and door areas will be excluded in the
results of surfaces.

```{r}
geom$area()[type == "Wall"]
geom$area(net = TRUE)[type == "Wall"]
```

## Get surface azimuth and tilt

```{r}
geom$azimuth()
geom$tilt()
```

# Convert simple geometry

`$convert()` generate detailed vertices from simplified geometry
specifications and replace the original object with its corresponding
detailed class, including:

* `BuildingSurface:Detailed`
* `FenestrationSurface:Detailed`
* `Shading:Site:Detailed`
* `Shading:Building:Detailed`
* `Shading:Zone:Detailed`

```{r}
path_simple <- path_eplus_example(eplus_ver, "4ZoneWithShading_Simple_1.idf")
simple <- read_idf(path_simple)

simple$class_name(by_group = TRUE)["Thermal Zones and Surfaces"]

simple$geometry()$convert()

simple$class_name(by_group = TRUE)["Thermal Zones and Surfaces"]
```

An attribute named `mapping` is attached in the converted `Idf` object which
contains the meta data of objects before and after the conversion.

```{r}
attr(simple, "mapping")
```

# Change coordinate systems

`$coord_system()` converts all vertices of geometries into specified
coordinate systems, e.g. from world to relative, and vice versa.
Besides, it also updates the `GlobalGeometryRules` in parent [Idf]
accordingly.

```{r}
geom$rules()

geom$parent()$to_table("Floor 1 Cafe Slab")

geom$coord_system("world")

geom$parent()$to_table("Floor 1 Cafe Slab")
```

# Round vertices decimal digits

`$round_digits()` performs number rounding on vertices of detailed geometry
object vertices, e.g. `BuildingSurface:Detailed`,
`FenestrationSurface:Detailed` and etc.

`$round_digits()` may be useful for clean up IDF files generated using
OpenStudio which often gives vertices with long trailing digits.

```{r}
geom$round_digits(3)

geom$parent()$to_table("Floor 1 Cafe Slab")
```

# View geometry in 3D

`$view()` uses a Three.js/WebGL widget to visualize the IDF geometry in 3D in
a similar way as [OpenStudio](https://www.openstudio.net).

`$view()` returns an [IdfViewer] object which can be used to further
tweak the viewer scene.

In the browser viewer, the default mouse interactions are:

* Left button: Trackball
* Right button: Pan
* Wheel: Zoom
* Click: Select a surface
* Shift/Ctrl/Command-click: Select multiple surfaces
* Double-click: Isolate the current selection

```{r, eval = FALSE}
viewer <- geom$view()
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("geom-viewer_default.png")
```

## Tweak the view

The `IdfViewer` class provides a number of methods to tweak the view in a
similar style as the OpenStudio SketchUp Plugin:

| Method          | Functionality                                           |
| :---            | :---                                                    |
| `$background()` | Change background                                       |
| `$viewpoint()`  | Change the viewpoint                                    |
| `$mouse_mode()` | Change the mouse controls                               |
| `$axis()`       | Add or remove axis, or tweak the style of axis.         |
| `$ground()`     | Add or remove the ground, or tweak the style of ground. |
| `$wireframe()`  | Turn on/off wireframes.                                 |
| `$x_ray()`      | Turn on/of X-ray style.                                 |
| `$render_by()`  | Change how surfaces should be colored.                  |
| `$show()`       | Change what components/zones/surfaces to show           |
| `$color_by()`   | Map time-varying simulation results to model objects.    |
| `$results()`    | Attach an `EplusSql` or completed `EplusJob` directly.   |
| `$diagnostics()`| Enable geometry-quality checks and linked issue markers. |

Below shows the effects of each method:

### Change background

```{r, eval = FALSE}
viewer$background("grey50")
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("geom-viewer_background1.png")
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
viewer$background("white")
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("geom-viewer_background2.png")
```

### Change viewpoint

```{r, eval = FALSE}

```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("geom-viewer_viewpoint1.png")
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
viewer$viewpoint("iso")
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("geom-viewer_viewpoint2.png")
```

### Change axis style

```{r, eval = FALSE}
viewer$axis(width = 5)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("geom-viewer_axis.png")
```


```{r, echo = FALSE}

```

### Change ground style

```{r, eval = FALSE}

```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("geom-viewer_ground.png")
```

### Turn on/off X-ray style

```{r, eval = FALSE}
viewer$x_ray(TRUE)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("geom-viewer_xray.png")
```


```{r, echo = FALSE}

```

### Change render style

```{r, eval = FALSE}

```


## Save the snapshot

`$snapshot()` saves the interactive widget as HTML or captures it as a PNG.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
viewer$show()
viewer$snapshot("view.png")
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("geom-viewer_ground.png")
```

## Work with the viewer widget

`$win_size()` controls the widget size. `$focus()` displays the current widget
again, and `$close()` forgets the current widget instance.

# Summary

The `IdfGeometry` and `IdfViewer` classes provide utilities to work and
visualize model geometries.

Currently, `IdfGeometry` is still evolving and more
methods will be added to perform geometric transformations in the near future.

Simulation results can be colored dynamically with `$color_by()`. Multiple
variables can be switched, stepped, searched, played back, and aggregated to
daily or monthly means in the browser. `$results()` can also attach an
`EplusSql` or completed `EplusJob` directly; its Shiny kernel mode asks DuckDB
for only the active variable and requested frame group and returns one compact
binary object-value frame. `$diagnostics()` links issue markers and affected
objects for adjacency gaps, duplicate or overlapping surfaces, non-planarity,
reversed normals, self-intersections, and subsurfaces outside their parents.


## Read-only views with a live R connection

The widget displays existing geometry. Selection, filtering, clipping and result
coloring do not change the IDF. It has no geometry editor or simulation runner.

The ordinary widget is portable and needs no R service after rendering. Opt into
a lightweight loopback connection when R should update the open view or read
selections. The listener runs in the current R session and closes with the viewer.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
viewer <- idf_viewer(idf)
viewer$on_select(function(objects) print(objects[, c("id", "name", "zone_name")]))
widget <- viewer$widget(live = TRUE)
widget

# These commands update the same browser view.
viewer$select(zone = "Zone 1")
viewer$filter(zone = "Zone 1", type = c("wall", "window"))
viewer$render_by("zone")
viewer$selection()
viewer$state()  # connection and command acknowledgement status
viewer$filter()  # remove live filters
```

R callbacks run while R is idle, or when the event loop is serviced. Commands are
asynchronous; the acknowledgement counter in `$state()` distinguishes sending
an update from completing it. Separate viewer objects have independent channels.
Use surface, Space or Zone selection mode in the widget to choose the pick scope.

Existing numerical results can be attached before or after opening a live view:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
viewer$color_by(zone_results, value = "temperature", object = "zone",
    key = "zone", time = "datetime", units = "degC")
viewer$update("time", frame = 0L)  # browser frame indices start at zero

# Read completed EnergyPlus outputs; this does not run a simulation.
viewer$results(sql, variable = "Zone Mean Air Temperature", mode = "provider")
viewer$close()
```

Zone values are repeated across their member surfaces for display; they are not
surface temperatures or an interpolated room temperature field. Use results from
the model being displayed. A portable HTML export requires embedded results and
contains no live connection. `$snapshot()` exports the configured scene; the
widget's screenshot button captures the current browser camera and visible scene.
